paras: The lynching of a Mexican man near Loma Parda, New Mexico, took place on November 13, 1882, when he was hanged for the alleged murder of a Fort Union soldier of the 23rd infantry. Accounts differ on whether soldiers or 'unknown parties' hanged him, and a later western-news brief said he had been proved innocent.

About a week before the lynching, a soldier from Fort Union, named James Gay by one report and private Frank Gay of Company A, 23rd infantry, by another, was killed at a dance at Loma Parda. The Las Vegas Daily Gazette's Fort Union correspondent called the killing a 'cowardly and brutal crime'.

According to that correspondent, Gay's comrades organized a posse, found the accused man in a shanty about three miles from the village where he had taken refuge, and on Monday hanged him from a projecting cliff. Three days later a letter to the Gazette signed 'Judge' gave a different version: the man was taken out of his bed, in his wife's presence, and hanged to a tree between Loma Parda and Fort Union by 'unknown parties'. The letter called the Las Vegas Optic's statement that soldiers took him from a dance hall false.
A brief printed in December added that 'indignant' soldiers burned his house and destroyed his haystack.

The same brief reported that it had since been proved the man was not guilty and that the people of Loma Parda were indignant at the soldiers' 'hasty conduct'. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage, and the lynched man is not named in any account.

The first reports were local items in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette, which called the hanging a 'choking bee', described the accused as 'the murderer' and 'the villain', and praised 'the boys in biue' for hunting him out. The 'Judge' letter likewise treated the man as guilty, saying the hanging saved 'costs for judge and jury', and used the case to attack the editor of the rival Optic.

Outside the territory the story ran only as a short item among New Mexico notes in the Omaha Daily Bee on December 7 and the Dillon Tribune of Montana on December 9, with the town's name garbled as 'Voma Porrta' and 'Loma Porda'. Unlike the Gazette, that brief presented the man as innocent and the soldiers as hasty.

The Gazette correspondent and the December brief named soldiers as the lynchers, while the 'Judge' letter attributed the hanging to 'unknown parties' and denied that soldiers took him. The reports also differ on where he was seized, a shanty or his own bed, and where he was hanged, a cliff or a tree.

reader.title: Lynching of a Mexican man near Loma Parda, New Mexico
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A Mexican man accused of killing a soldier was hanged by a soldiers' posse (A1, A3) or by 'unknown parties' (A2) without trial.

All three independent reports say the man was lynched or hanged for the alleged murder of a soldier, by a 'posse' of the soldier's comrades (A1), 'indignant' soldiers (A3) or 'unknown parties' who thereby saved 'costs for judge and jury' (A2); no lawful authority is mentioned.
Two local Las Vegas Gazette items (A1, A2) and a separate western-news brief (A3) agree that the accused man was lynched near Loma Parda, though they differ on who did it and where he was seized.

accounts.label: Fort Union correspondent
accounts.gist: Soldier James Gay's comrades formed a posse, hunted the accused out of a shanty three miles from the village and hanged him from a projecting cliff on Monday.

accounts.label: Letter signed 'Judge'
accounts.gist: The man was taken from his bed and his wife and hanged to a tree by 'unknown parties', not taken from a dance hall by soldiers as the Las Vegas Optic had said.

accounts.label: Western-news brief
accounts.gist: Indignant soldiers lynched the man and burned his house and haystack; it was later proved he was not guilty, and Loma Parda residents were indignant at the soldiers.

framing.detail: The Gazette's local column called the hanging a 'choking bee', the killing of Gay a 'cowardly and brutal crime', and the accused 'the villain' whom 'the boys in biue hunted' out.
The 'Judge' letter called the killing of Gay 'cruel' and 'dastardly' and said the lynching saved 'costs for judge and jury'.
The Omaha Bee and Dillon Tribune brief, under state-by-state jottings, reported the man innocent and the townspeople indignant at the soldiers' 'hasty conduct'.
